title: Beating The Scandinavian Defense | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The pawn to e4, d5 — the Scandinavian.
We take on d5.
The queen recaptures — multiple options in the Scandinavian.
The knight to c3 — d4 is far less common but also good; everybody plays the knight to c3, so that's what we do.
The queen to a5. I want to teach you an uncommon setup that'll surprise people — most play d4, some the trappy b4 — but I'll play a move that makes a lot of you roll your eyes —
— g3, preparing to fianchetto; it's an easy system, heavy on good positional principles.
c6, the bishop to g2. Once you fianchetto, the knight comes to e2 so as not to obstruct the bishop. It might seem the bishop is biting on granite —
— but the second component of this setup is where this bishop, assuming the game goes along normal lines, becomes a very good piece.
The knight to e2 — White has a plan that involves breaking down the c-pawn and getting this bishop to operate at full potential.
e5, and we castle — just the normal developing moves, d3, nothing much to say; once development is complete I'll show the main plan.

The bishop to b4 isn't great — usually people play e6; I'm less familiar with e5, which could let us play d4 and challenge the centre. The bishop to b4 walks right into a move we'd have played anyway.
a3 — a natural reaction to the bishop to b4; e5 was a bit loosey-goosey. a3 doesn't threaten to take the bishop —
— but he takes anyway. Neither the b-pawn nor the d-pawn recapture is worth ruining our pawn structure —
— we take with the knight. Now, what are we preparing with a3? Ask it that way and you should see the plan —
— the plan is to push the b-pawn to b5, a classic minority attack of sorts, getting this bishop to fire on all cylinders. The bishop to g4.
We don't want f3, and definitely not the bishop to f3 — we want the queen to e1, and later chase the bishop away with h3.
If Black castles, are we in a huge rush to play b4? No — knowing your plan doesn't mean carrying it out immediately; it's fine to complete development first and carry out the plan when you're ready.

You could play b4, but I like the more patient d3; don't reveal your hand too soon, especially when there's no way to stop b4 — c5 would be horrendous and does our work for us. Maybe we'll want the bishop to g5 first, for a kingside attack.
Black's best here is the knight from b8 to d7, completing development. I don't want the bishop to d2 — it's counterproductive, because it helps Black's queen get away from a5.

That defeats part of the purpose of b4, which is that it's a move with tempo. So now we play b4, which also opens a very attractive developing square on b2 for the bishop — a double fianchetto — pressuring the e5-pawn. The knight on c3 will eventually move; don't hesitate to put a piece on a square another of your pieces covers.

The knight will go to e4, or maybe stay; the bishop has a lot of potential energy. The queen to a6 is very strange — trying to prevent b5, but this queen goes offside, and we reinforce b5 with a later a4.

Why not kick the bishop with h3? Fine, but the bishop isn't truly bothering me on g4; I'll throw it in to force a decision, though I wouldn't in a classical game, since it lets the bishop reposition. When Black's bishop lands on f5, watch for e4 later — we have a queen on e1 and an x-ray — though e4 isn't immediately possible, with four defenders against three attackers.
It's very hard for Black to reinforce that square, because the queen is so out of the game it can't easily get to e7.
The bishop to h5 is something I like to see; now let's complete development with the bishop to b2.
Some of you might have been attracted to the bishop to g5, but —

— that's not dangerous, since Black plays the knight to d7 and you'd go anyway, which makes no sense. One interesting bit of practice in not stopping calculation prematurely: whenever you have a bishop on the long diagonal, be aware of building a battery — imagine the knights on f6 and c3 both gone from the board; then the queen to c3 becomes a really nasty battery, forcing a weakening move like f6.
How should we capture the pawn? Taking with the pawn and then f4 and e5 is one very powerful approach, but I like the knight takes e4, which is probably worse than the d-pawn recapture —
— but I want to emphasize an idea. Do we take automatically with a pawn? Does the bishop takes e4 lose the bishop to f5? No, it does not —
— because of the queen to c3, setting a trap. This is how you set traps: you make moves good on their own merit, and I can almost guarantee f5 will happen, fast. The queen to c3 threatens mate —
— and in the event of f5 it's a total disaster, Black losing that pawn. Hard to predict, but the rook takes e4 — this is just total collapse.
It's not good to play the whole game without developing your queenside — that went down the drain very quickly. g3 is one of several —
— good, underrated systems —
— good and, in my opinion, underrated systems against the —
— the knight to f6, the knight to e2 —
— Scandinavian. e5 is possible, but generally Black —
— goes the bishop to f5 —
— and then puts the pawn on e6; in the Scandinavian it's not about controlling the most squares but building up a very solid centre.
It might be that e5 is a reasonable move as well.

So e5, castles, the bishop to b4 is already inaccurate, walking into a3. I'd get the bishop out to d6, but many are tempted by the bishop to c5 — on flexibility, usually you play d3, but if the bishop lands here you can go a3 and the rook to b1 to prepare b4; or, as I'm thinking, d4: the bishop walks into it, and after the pawns trade and the knight recaptures, Black faces concrete problems — two nasty threats, one being the knight to b3, which doesn't merely trade knight for bishop, and if the queen stays with the queen to b6, the knight to a4 wins.
